units.title: Unit 41 — Sound
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 86–87 (PDF pages 90–91).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
learningObjectives: Describe natural soundscapes with accurate verb–noun and adjective–noun combinations.
Distinguish loud, sharp, soft and continuous sounds, including register and implied intensity.
Describe the sounds made by people, animals, vehicles and machines with natural collocations.
Use give and make appropriately with cries, reactions and sound nouns.

items.pt: um silêncio assustador; um silêncio inquietante
items.example: An eerie silence filled the empty school after sunset.
items.note: Eerie suggests a mysterious or unsettling quiet atmosphere, not simply the absence of noise.

items.pt: um estrondo distante de trovão; um ribombar de trovão
items.example: We heard a rumble of thunder as the clouds gathered.
items.note: Rumble suggests a deep, rolling sound; it often refers to distant thunder.

items.word: the wind whistles through the trees
items.pt: o vento assobia entre as árvores
items.example: At night, the wind whistles through the trees behind our house.
items.note: Whistle describes the high sound air makes as it passes through a narrow space.

items.pt: ondas quebram com força na praia
items.example: During the storm, huge waves crashed on the beach.
items.note: Crash emphasises the loud, forceful impact of waves; this is not the normal choice for gentle ripples.

items.pt: um riacho murmurante; um riacho de águas borbulhantes
items.example: We sat beside a babbling stream and ate lunch.
items.note: Babbling describes the pleasant, continuous sound of water flowing over stones.

items.example: Birds sing outside our window every morning.
items.note: Sing is the ordinary verb for melodic bird sounds.

items.pt: o tamborilar da chuva; o som de pingos de chuva
items.example: The patter of rain on the roof helped me fall asleep.
items.note: Patter is the repeated, fairly light tapping of raindrops on a surface.

items.example: A distant car horn broke the silence of the village.
items.note: Something audible interrupts a period of quiet; do not say close the silence.

items.example: Two shots rang out across the valley.
items.note: Ring out describes a sudden, clear, resonant sound, especially a shot or bell.

items.example: A piercing cry came from the injured bird.
items.note: Piercing refers to a very sharp, high sound that is hard to ignore.

items.example: The speakers produced a deafening sound during the concert.
items.note: Deafening describes a sound so loud that it is painful or makes other sounds hard to hear.

items.pt: um barulho ensurdecedor; um ruído estridente
items.example: The alarm made an ear-splitting noise in the corridor.
items.note: Ear-splitting strongly emphasises sudden, extremely unpleasant loudness.

items.example: Residents complained about excessive noise from the nightclub.
items.note: Excessive means more than is reasonable or acceptable; noise is uncountable here.

items.example: I switched off the fan to reduce the background noise on the call.
items.note: Background noise is sound present behind the main conversation or activity.

items.example: We heard a muffled sound through the closed door.
items.note: Muffled means made less clear or less loud by a barrier or covering.

items.example: The actor used a shrill voice to play the frightened character.
items.note: Shrill combines a high pitch with an often unpleasant quality.

items.example: Her shrill laugh could be heard from the other end of the room.
items.note: Shrill also collocates with laugh, particularly when the pitch is unusually high.

items.pt: gargalhadas altas e estridentes; risadas escandalosas
items.example: Raucous laughter came from the crowded café.
items.note: Raucous suggests noisy, rough, unrestrained laughter, not a quiet giggle.

items.example: The suitcase landed on the carpet with a dull thud.
items.note: A dull thud is a low, non-ringing impact sound, often from something heavy landing on a soft surface.

items.example: The old gate made a grating noise when it opened.
items.note: Grating describes a harsh, scraping sound that people generally find unpleasant.

items.pt: um estrondo alto; um forte estampido
items.example: A loud bang woke everyone in the house.
items.note: Bang is a sudden impact or explosive sound; loud is a neutral intensity description.

items.pt: um estrondo tremendo; um estouro ensurdecedor
items.example: We heard an almighty bang when the metal door slammed shut.
items.note: Almighty is an informal emphatic intensifier, usually suggesting exceptional loudness.

items.pt: uma explosão barulhenta; um forte estrondo de explosão
items.example: A loud explosion shook the windows in the distance.
items.note: Loud combines naturally with explosion; the sound is sudden and powerful.

items.example: The film ended with an almighty explosion in the final scene.
items.note: Almighty is expressive and relatively informal; it stresses unusual force or volume.

items.pt: o rugido do trânsito; o ruído intenso do tráfego
items.example: The roar of traffic made it difficult to sleep near the motorway.
items.note: Roar describes the continuous, powerful noise of many moving vehicles.

items.pt: a música toca muito alto; a música estronda
items.example: Music blared out of the shop late into the evening.
items.note: Blare out means to be played extremely loudly, often unpleasantly.

items.pt: o rádio toca alto demais; o rádio estronda
items.example: The radio blared from the kitchen all morning.
items.note: A radio can blare when it plays very loudly; blare out is also used when describing the sound being emitted.

items.pt: máquinas zumbem; máquinas fazem um zumbido constante
items.example: Several machines hummed quietly in the laboratory.
items.note: Hum is a steady, low, continuous sound from equipment or engines.

items.pt: máquinas fazem um zumbido suave de funcionamento
items.example: The small machines whirred as their motors started.
items.note: Whirr is a low, continuous mechanical sound, often from something rotating.

items.example: She gave a sigh of relief when the test finished.
items.note: Give a sigh is a conventional way to describe producing an audible breath, often from emotion.

items.example: He gave a short laugh at the surprising suggestion.
items.note: Give a laugh focuses on one act of laughing rather than the general activity.

items.example: The child gave a loud cry when the balloon burst.
items.note: Give a cry means let out a vocal expression, often suddenly.

items.example: She gave a cry of pain when she touched the hot pan.
items.note: Of pain specifies the feeling expressed by the cry.

items.example: He gave a cry of surprise when he saw the unexpected visitor.
items.note: Cry of surprise can express an emotional reaction without necessarily suggesting distress.

items.pt: dar um grito de alarme; gritar em sinal de alerta
items.example: A passenger gave a cry of alarm when smoke appeared.
items.note: Cry of alarm expresses fear or warning in response to danger.

items.pt: soltar um suspiro brusco; emitir um arquejo
items.example: The audience gave a gasp when the acrobat slipped.
items.note: A gasp is a sudden, audible intake of breath, often expressing shock.

items.example: He gave a groan as he tried to lift the heavy box.
items.note: A groan is a low sound expressing effort, pain or dissatisfaction.

items.pt: produzir um som de arranhão; fazer um ruído de raspagem
items.example: The cat made a scratching sound against the wooden door.
items.note: Scratching suggests a rough, repeated contact against a surface.

items.pt: produzir um som de clique; fazer um estalo
items.example: The faulty switch made a clicking sound every few seconds.
items.note: Clicking is a small, sharp, repeated sound, often from a mechanism.

items.pt: fazer um som de farfalhar; produzir um ruído de folhas ou papel
items.example: Dry leaves made a rustling sound under our feet.
items.note: Rustling describes the light noise of moving paper, leaves or fabric.

items.pt: produzir um som crepitante; fazer estalidos
items.example: The burning logs made a crackling sound in the fireplace.
items.note: Crackling is a series of small, rapid, sharp sounds, especially from fire.

items.example: A groan of disappointment spread through the crowd when the match was cancelled.
items.note: The noun groan can be followed by of disappointment to specify the emotion.

items.pt: motocicletas passam rugindo; motos passam fazendo muito barulho
items.example: Several motorbikes roared past the café at midnight.
items.note: Roar past combines loud engine noise with movement; the sound is more forceful than a hum.

units.title: Unit 42 — Distance and size
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 88–89 (PDF pages 92–93).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Basic concepts · distance, quantity and size
learningObjectives: Describe proximity and travel distances with the correct lexical partners and prepositions.
Differentiate low, small, large, little, high and tall in conventional word combinations.
Talk naturally about the scale of objects, amounts and personal characteristics.
Express the size or importance of differences and changes with major and minor.

items.example: The village is a considerable distance from the nearest hospital.
items.note: Considerable distance means quite a long way; retain from before the reference point.

items.example: Our campsite was a long distance from the main road.
items.note: Long indicates substantial separation; from introduces the place of reference.

items.example: The station is a short distance from the university.
items.note: Short distance means nearby, without implying an exact number of metres.

items.pt: a uma distância viável para ir e voltar do trabalho
items.example: We looked for a flat within commuting distance of the factory.
items.note: Refers to being close enough to travel to work regularly; usually followed by of.

items.pt: a uma distância que pode ser percorrida a pé
items.example: The supermarket is within walking distance of our house.
items.note: A location within walking distance is near enough to reach on foot.

items.example: The hikers covered a distance of 40 kilometres in two days.
items.note: Cover describes completing a measured distance; the number here illustrates a replaceable quantity.

items.example: The team travelled a distance of 50 kilometres to reach the site.
items.note: Travel a distance of is a normal way to state how far someone goes; the quantity can vary.

items.example: As a child, she dreamed of exploring far-off places.
items.note: Far-off is an attributive adjective meaning distant or remote.

items.pt: destinos longínquos; destinos nos lugares mais distantes
items.example: Their travel agency specialises in far-flung destinations.
items.note: Far-flung suggests distant and sometimes widely scattered locations.

items.pt: de muito perto; a curta distância
items.example: The photographer captured the bird at close range.
items.note: Refers to a very short physical distance, particularly when viewing or photographing something.

items.example: Many people commute to the capital from neighbouring towns.
items.note: Neighbouring describes towns situated next to or very near another place.

items.example: The rail network connects several neighbouring countries.
items.note: Neighbouring countries share a border or are situated adjacent to one another.

items.example: Flood warnings were issued for neighbouring areas.
items.note: Neighbouring modifies a nearby geographical area, not a distant region.

items.example: Customers were attracted by the shop's low prices.
items.note: Say low prices, not small prices, when describing how inexpensive something is.

items.example: Workers protested against low wages and unsafe conditions.
items.note: Low is the natural adjective for wages; small wages is not the normal combination.

items.example: Scientists measured low levels of contamination in the water.
items.note: Use low to describe a level on a scale, rather than small levels.

items.example: The recipe uses small quantities of salt and sugar.
items.note: Small modifies quantities, whereas little quantities is not idiomatic.

items.example: Small numbers of visitors arrived during the winter.
items.note: Small numbers describes a low count; little numbers is unnatural.

items.example: Only small amounts of water leaked from the pipe.
items.note: With amounts, use small or large, not little as an adjective before the noun.

items.example: There was a small increase in demand after the launch.
items.note: The natural adjective with increase is small; little increase can mean almost no increase in other constructions.

items.example: The warehouse stores large quantities of grain.
items.note: Large is the normal opposite of small with quantities.

items.example: Large numbers of students attended the open day.
items.note: Use large numbers of with plural countable nouns.

items.example: The project requires large amounts of energy.
items.note: Large amounts of typically combines with mass or abstract uncountable nouns.

items.pt: um grande aumento; um aumento expressivo
items.example: The city reported a large increase in public transport use.
items.note: Large describes the extent of an increase.

items.example: The company now produces batteries on a large scale.
items.note: On a large scale describes an activity performed extensively.

items.example: The researchers tested the method on a small scale first.
items.note: On a small scale indicates limited scope, quantity or operation.

items.example: Our town faces the same problem, but on a smaller scale.
items.note: The comparative form is useful when comparing the scope of two situations.

items.pt: um mapa de grande escala; mapa com mais detalhes de uma área menor
items.example: We used a large-scale map to find the narrow paths around the village.
items.note: A large-scale map shows a relatively small area in substantial detail; hyphenation is common before a noun.

items.pt: pobrezinha da criança; pobre criança pequena
items.example: The teacher comforted the poor little child after the accident.
items.note: Poor little can convey sympathy or affection in informal speech; poor here does not necessarily mean without money.

items.example: Their dear little dog always waits at the front door.
items.note: Dear little adds affection to an informal description.

items.pt: quartinho agradável; cômodo pequeno e aconchegante
items.example: We found a nice little room above the bakery.
items.note: Nice little often sounds warmly appreciative, not necessarily dismissive.

items.example: My little brother started secondary school this year.
items.note: Little can mean younger, not necessarily physically smaller; informal family usage.

items.example: Her big brother taught her how to ride a bicycle.
items.note: Big brother is the informal counterpart of little brother in terms of age.

items.example: We've got a little problem with the booking system.
items.note: Little can downplay the importance of a problem; tone and context affect interpretation.

items.pt: pequenas tarefas para fazer; coisinhas para resolver
items.example: I have a few little things to do before dinner.
items.note: Little things is natural in informal English for minor tasks or matters.

items.example: The manager tried to make him look small in front of his colleagues.
items.note: Make someone look small is an idiom for making them feel or appear inferior, not for changing physical size.

items.pt: jogar conversa fora; conversar sobre amenidades
items.example: We made small talk while waiting for the meeting to start.
items.note: Small talk is polite conversation about unimportant or non-personal subjects; use make, not do.

items.pt: um livro grosso; um livro volumoso
items.example: I borrowed a fat book about medieval history.
items.note: Fat can informally describe a thick book; plump is for people, not books.

items.pt: um livro fino; um livro de poucas páginas
items.example: The guide is a slim book that fits in a coat pocket.
items.note: Slim can describe both a thin book and a slender person.

items.example: The story describes a fat person sitting beside the window.
items.note: Fat can describe body size but may sound blunt or impolite when used about people.

items.pt: uma pessoa esbelta; uma pessoa magra
items.example: The tailor designed the suit for a slim person.
items.note: Slim is generally positive or neutral when describing a person's build.

items.example: The portrait showed a plump person with rosy cheeks.
items.note: Plump is usually a milder, sometimes affectionate term for a round body shape; not used of a book.

items.example: The drawing shows a skinny person wearing an oversized coat.
items.note: Skinny can suggest someone is too thin and may be negative, depending on context.

items.example: The neglected dog was painfully thin when it was rescued.
items.note: Painfully intensifies thin to suggest an extreme or worrying degree.

items.example: She spent a great deal of time preparing the presentation.
items.note: A great deal of combines naturally with the uncountable noun time; not a big deal of time.

items.example: The renovation cost a great deal of money.
items.note: A great deal of marks a large amount of an uncountable noun such as money.

items.example: Running a small business takes a great deal of energy.
items.note: Use a great deal of with energy as an uncountable resource.

items.example: The volunteers showed a great deal of enthusiasm for the project.
items.note: Enthusiasm is uncountable here; a great deal of is the idiomatic quantity expression.

items.example: There is a major difference between the two designs.
items.note: Major expresses importance or magnitude, rather than physical size.

items.example: The two versions have only a minor difference in wording.
items.note: Minor contrasts with major and means relatively unimportant.

items.example: The new policy represents a major change for employees.
items.note: Major can indicate that the effect or scope of a change is substantial.

items.example: We made a minor change to the wiring diagram.
items.note: A minor change is limited in scope or significance.

items.example: The price increase had a major effect on sales.
items.note: A major effect is a highly significant consequence.

items.example: The delay had only a minor effect on the schedule.
items.note: A minor effect is limited in magnitude or importance.

items.example: Funding remains a major difficulty for the programme.
items.note: Major is natural with difficulty when the obstacle is significant.

items.example: We had a minor difficulty installing the update.
items.note: Minor softens the seriousness of a problem.

items.example: The speaker made a major point about long-term maintenance.
items.note: Major can refer to a central or particularly important point in an argument.

items.example: There is one minor point I'd like to clarify before we finish.
items.note: Minor point signals a detail of relatively little importance.

items.example: The report highlights several major issues with the plan.
items.note: Major issues are significant matters requiring attention.

items.pt: questões menores; problemas de pouca gravidade
items.example: The software passed the tests apart from a few minor issues.
items.note: Minor issues are relatively small problems rather than serious faults.

items.example: Cost was a major factor in their decision.
items.note: Major factor means an important influence on an outcome.

items.example: Weather was only a minor factor in the final result.
items.note: Minor describes a limited or secondary contribution.

items.section: D · Common mistakes: tall and high
items.example: Tall people may need more legroom on long flights.
items.note: Tall describes the height of people; high people does not mean physically tall.

items.section: D · Common mistakes: tall and high
items.example: Tall trees shade the garden in summer.
items.note: Tall is natural for the vertical growth of trees.

items.section: D · Common mistakes: tall and high
items.example: Tall buildings surround the old railway station.
items.note: Tall is standard for the height of buildings.

items.section: D · Common mistakes: tall and high
items.example: High mountains were visible beyond the valley.
items.note: High is the natural modifier for mountains rather than tall.

items.section: D · Common mistakes: tall and high
items.example: High prices discouraged buyers this month.
items.note: Say high prices, not tall prices.

items.section: D · Common mistakes: tall and high
items.example: High interest rates can make borrowing expensive.
items.note: High modifies interest rates; it contrasts with low interest rates.

items.section: D · Common mistakes: tall and high
items.example: Low interest rates reduced the cost of the loan.
items.note: Low interest rates are the opposite of high ones, not short interest rates.

items.section: D · Common mistakes: tall and high
items.example: She wore high heels to the ceremony.
items.note: High heels describes shoes or their tall raised heels, not the height of a person.

items.section: D · Common mistakes: tall and high
items.example: I prefer shoes with low heels when I have to walk a lot.
items.note: Low heels contrasts with high heels; the phrase refers to the height of a shoe's heel.

items.section: D · Common mistakes: tall and high
items.example: The beach almost disappeared at high tide.
items.note: High tide is the stage when the sea reaches its upper level along the shore.

items.section: D · Common mistakes: tall and high
items.example: She practises the high jump at the athletics club.
items.note: High jump is the name of an athletics event, not a way to describe a tall person.
